notes:
I've written notes for most verses, but several parts of your list are missing. My search tool hit its usage limit partway through, so I couldn't reach any Lutheran, Catholic, Orthodox, Pentecostal-denominational (ag.org), netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org or prosperity / word-of-faith sources. Verses 30, 31, 34, 53 and 54 have no notes. Several other verses rest on only one or two commentators.

Tradition labels: StudyLight itself tags Calvin as "Calvinist", Wesley as "Arminian" and Coffman as "Arminian / Restoration Movement". The labels for Gill, Clarke, MacLaren and Piper are my own identifications, not something the pages state.

---

**v. 29**
- Martha said Jesus was calling for Mary. Guzik quotes Tenney: Mary took this as a command and went at once. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-11/

**v. 32**
- Mary's words are almost the same as Martha's in v. 21. Guzik quotes Bruce suggesting the sisters had probably said this to each other many times. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-11/
- Guzik says we can't hear her tone. It could be a statement of faith that Jesus would have healed Lazarus, or a criticism that He came late. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-11/
- Barclay also notes that Mary's greeting matches Martha's. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dsb/john-11.html
- Wesley: Mary fell at Jesus' feet, which Martha had not done, making up for coming more slowly. https://ccel.org/ccel/wesley/notes.i.v.xii.html

**v. 33** (traditions differ on Jesus' emotion)
- *Anger at death:* Guzik, citing Morris, says the Greek verb is properly used of horses snorting and usually means anger when used of people. In his view Jesus was angry at death, humanity's great enemy. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-11/
- GotQuestions says the word appears elsewhere only of Jesus and expresses outrage, a reaction to sin and death. It adds that "spirit" here means Jesus' inner being, not the Holy Spirit. https://www.gotquestions.org/groan-in-the-spirit.html (also reproduced at https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-11-commentary)
- The bible.org exegetical commentary says the verb shows strong emotion that is hard to translate, something like "shuddered". https://bible.org/seriespage/exegetical-commentary-john-11
- *Methodist (Wesley):* Groaning was how Jesus held back His tears. Wesley says Jesus' feelings were not uncontrolled passions but voluntary emotions, fully in His power. https://ccel.org/ccel/wesley/notes.i.v.xii.html
- *Contrast, Barclay:* He describes the groan as involuntary, bursting from Jesus as He trembled with emotion. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dsb/john-11.html
- *Reformed (Calvin):* By His groaning and tears, Jesus shows He is as affected by our troubles as if He bore them Himself. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/11-33.html
- *Gill:* The Jews may have wept out of sympathy, or hypocritically. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/11-33.html
- Guzik quotes Barclay that Jewish mourning was loud wailing, since more weeping was thought to honour the dead more. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-11/

**v. 35** (traditions differ on why Jesus wept)
- *The word itself:* It differs from the loud wailing of v. 33 and means quiet tears. Jesus was deeply moved but not out of control (Guzik, quoting Morris). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-11/ Bible.org says the same. https://bible.org/seriespage/exegetical-commentary-john-11
- *Matthew Henry:* It shows Jesus was truly human, with a human soul. As a man He could weep, and as a merciful man He would, before He showed His divinity. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jhn/Jhn_011.cfm
- *Spurgeon:* This was divine sympathy, and it is not wrong for believers to grieve even though they hope for resurrection. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/john-11.html and https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-11/
- *Wesley:* Jesus wept from sympathy with the mourners and from a deep sense of the misery sin has brought on human nature. https://ccel.org/ccel/wesley/notes.i.v.xii.html
- *Not grief for Lazarus himself:*
  - Constable says it was sorrow over sin and its results, since Jesus was about to restore Lazarus. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/11-35.html
  - Bible.org says it was grief over sin, death and Satan's realm. It mentions Morris's view (grief at the bystanders' misunderstanding) and the possibility that Jesus foresaw His own tomb. https://bible.org/seriespage/exegetical-commentary-john-11
  - Chuck Smith (Calvary Chapel) bluntly calls it "ridiculous" to think Jesus wept because Lazarus died. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/11-35.html
- *A minority view, Coffman (Restoration Movement):* Jesus may have wept because He was calling back to a dangerous world someone who had already won the crown of life. https://studylight.org/commentaries/bcc/john-11.html
- Barclay: Greek readers would have been astonished that the Son of God could weep. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dsb/john-11.html
- Precept Austin contrasts these quiet tears with Jesus' loud weeping over Jerusalem (Luke 19:41). https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-11-commentary

**v. 36**
- Spurgeon: Believers are not mere onlookers to this love but share in Christ's special love. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/john-11.html

**v. 37** (readings differ)
- Guzik reads the remark as genuine sorrow and sympathy. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-11/
- Wesley calls it a strange mixture of faith and unbelief, since they never imagined Jesus could raise Lazarus. https://ccel.org/ccel/wesley/notes.i.v.xii.html
- GotQuestions says the onlookers' spiritual blindness and unbelief deepened Jesus' distress (vv. 37–38). https://www.gotquestions.org/groan-in-the-spirit.html

**v. 38**
- Wesley: Cave tombs were common, as with the patriarchs at Machpelah. They were cut into rock and closed with a large stone. https://ccel.org/ccel/wesley/notes.i.v.xii.html

**v. 39**
- Wesley: In Martha's words, reason and faith struggle together. https://ccel.org/ccel/wesley/notes.i.v.xii.html

**v. 40**
- Bible.org: Revealing God's glory is the main purpose of the miracle, recalling v. 4. https://bible.org/seriespage/exegetical-commentary-john-11
- Wesley: This shows Jesus had told Martha more than John records. https://ccel.org/ccel/wesley/notes.i.v.xii.html

**vv. 41–42**
- Wesley: Jesus was not asking His Father for help. He acted with complete sovereignty as Lord of life and death, thanking the Father for this chance to show His power and God's praise. https://ccel.org/ccel/wesley/notes.i.v.xii.html

**v. 43**
- Guzik: Jesus simply called Lazarus out, while others in Scripture who raised the dead used more elaborate methods. He quotes Trench that "loud voice" in John means a decisive tone of authority. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-11/
- Matthew Henry: People speak loudly to wake a sleeper, and the loud voice fulfils Isaiah 45:19. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jhn/Jhn_011.cfm
- Wesley: Jesus spoke loudly so everyone present could hear, and called Lazarus as easily as if he were awake. https://ccel.org/ccel/wesley/notes.i.v.xii.html

**v. 44**
- Wesley: If Jews buried as Egyptians did, the face cloth went round the forehead and chin, so Lazarus could see his way. https://ccel.org/ccel/wesley/notes.i.v.xii.html
- Precept Austin: This was a resuscitation (Lazarus would die again), not a resurrection. It connects with John's theme of hearing Jesus' voice and living. https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-11-commentary

**v. 45**
- Wesley: Here the Son of God was glorified, as promised in v. 4. https://ccel.org/ccel/wesley/notes.i.v.xii.html

**v. 46**
- Wesley sees this as a sad confirmation of Luke 16:31: people who reject Moses won't be persuaded even if someone rises from the dead. https://ccel.org/ccel/wesley/notes.i.v.xii.html

**vv. 47–48**
- Wesley: The right answer to "What are we to do?" was to believe. Death gave way to Christ sooner than unbelief did. "Place" means the Temple and "nation" means both church and state. He thinks their fear of Rome was only a pretext, since one who raised the dead could defeat the Romans. https://ccel.org/ccel/wesley/notes.i.v.xii.html
- MacLaren: The leaders admit the miracles but their concern is pure self-interest, not patriotism or religion. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/11-49.htm

**v. 49**
- Ellicott: Caiaphas (high priest AD 26–36) had the proper name Joseph. "That year" marks the fatal, decisive year. "You know nothing" probably dismisses other proposals in the council. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/11-49.htm
- Clarke notes that under Moses' law the high priesthood was for life (Ex. 40:15). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/11-49.html
- Wesley: "That year" was the memorable year of Christ's death. Caiaphas was rebuking the council's slow deliberation. https://ccel.org/ccel/wesley/notes.i.v.xii.html
- Benson, citing Campbell: Caiaphas was faulting their lack of political wisdom, not their knowledge of the law. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/11-49.htm
- Barclay calls the remark notoriously discourteous, and the Light of Israel commentary calls it rough and callous. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/11-49.html

**v. 50**
- Guzik: Caiaphas reasoned logically but not morally. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-11/
- Calvin: Caiaphas was in effect saying they must provoke God's wrath in order to prosper. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/11-49.html
- MacLaren develops a sermon warning religious professionals against judging truth by "what is expedient for us". https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/11-49.htm

**v. 51** (how Caiaphas could prophesy)
- *Because of his office:*
  - Guzik says John credits the office, not the man. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-11/
  - Ellicott says the high priest was God's official representative. Meyer links this to the high priest's old role with the Urim and Thummim. Poole says God overruled Caiaphas's tongue beyond his own intentions, as with Saul and Balaam. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/11-51.htm
- *Unconscious prophecy:*
  - Pulpit compares Balaam, Nebuchadnezzar and Pharaoh. https://biblehub.com/john/11-51.htm
  - Barnes says Caiaphas was not a true prophet, but his words state the truth of the atonement. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/11-51.htm
- *Wesley:* The spirit of prophecy overruled him. Caiaphas bore unknowing witness to Christ's priestly office, as Pilate did to His kingly office. https://ccel.org/ccel/wesley/notes.i.v.xii.html
- *Piper:* God planned Jesus' death from the start, and the verse teaches substitution. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/jesus-died-to-gather-the-children-of-god--2
- *MacLaren:* Christ died for that very nation, "for Caiaphas as truly as for John." Rejecting His death became the nation's ruin. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/11-49.htm

**v. 52** (the clearest difference between traditions: who are the "scattered children of God"?)
- *Reformed (Calvin):* The children of God are counted so by election, even before they are called and come to faith. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/11-52.html
- *Gill:* They are mainly the elect among the Gentiles, for whom Christ died. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/11-52.html
- *Piper:* Inside the universal offer of the gospel, God has a particular design to gather His chosen people, especially Gentiles, into one people (Rev. 5:9). https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/jesus-died-to-gather-the-children-of-god--2
- *Wesley:* All God's children "through all ages and nations", gathered into one Church. https://ccel.org/ccel/wesley/notes.i.v.xii.html
- *Clarke:* John probably meant only the Jews dispersed among the nations. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/11-52.html
- *MacLaren:* They are called children "by anticipation", since in John people become God's children through faith. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/john/11-49.htm
- *Others:*
  - Constable says they are Jews and Gentiles united in the church. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/john/11-52.html
  - Guzik links them to the "other sheep" of John 10:16. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-11/
  - A Guzik Q&A says that "the nation" in v. 51 means Israel, but John wanted it clear that Jesus did not die only for Israel. https://enduringword.com/correcting-my-mistakes-qa-for-january-6-2022/

**v. 55**
- Wesley: Pilgrims purified themselves to remove anything that would prevent them from eating the Passover. https://ccel.org/ccel/wesley/notes.i.v.xii.html

**vv. 56–57**
- Ellicott: Some manuscripts leave out a word, so read "Now the chief priests and the Pharisees had given commandment". The order explains the crowd's question: would Jesus come despite it? https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/john/11.htm
